items.title: Ashok Leyland reports 23% growth in October sales to 21,888 units
items.summary:
Commercial vehicle major Ashok Leyland on Monday reported a 23 per cent year-on-year growth in its total sales during October.
The Chennai-based automaker's total sales, including exports, stood at 21,888 units, up from 17,820 units a year ago, according to an exchange filing.
Sales in the Medium and Heavy Commercial Vehicle (M&HCV) segment grew 28 per cent to 13,927 units from 10,865 units, while the Light Commercial Vehicle (LCV) segment registered a 14 per cent rise to 7,961 units.
Total domestic sales rose 24 per cent to 20,224 units from 16,314 units a year ago, with 32 per cent growth in the M&HCV segment to 12,646 units. Domestic LCV sales increased 13 per cent to 7,578 units.

items.title: Cyclone Murasu tracker: Where is the storm now?
items.summary: Severe Cyclonic Storm Murasu moved west-northwestwards at a speed of 22 kmph over the west-central and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal during the six hours preceding 8:30 am IST on Monday, November 2, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said. At the time, the cyclone was centred near latitude 14.1°N and longitude 81.4°E, approximately 160 km east-southeast of Nellore, 180 km northeast of Chennai, 180 km east-southeast of Kavali, 210 km southeast of Ongole and 240 km south of Machilipatnam.The IMD said Murasu is likely to continue moving northwestwards and cross the south Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm, with sustained wind speeds of 100–110 kmph and gusts reaching 120 kmph. Landfall is expected between Nellore and Narsapur, south of Ongole, from around 11:30 pm on November 2 to the early hours of November 3, 2026.The IMD has warned of heavy rainfall and strong winds along the storm's projected path. Southern Odisha is also expected to receive heavy rainfall, prompting disaster response teams to remain prepared in vulnerable areas.— Indiametdept (@Indiametdept) Also Read: Weather today, November 2: IMD warns of heavy rain in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu; Delhi-NCR's AQI becomes 'severe'; check latest IMD update and AQI levelsCyclone Murasu tracker: Where is the storm now?As of 5:30 am on November 2, Murasu was positioned over the west-central and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal, near 13.9°N latitude and 81.8°E longitude. It had moved west-northwestwards at 25 kmph during the previous six hours and was approximately 200 km from Chennai.The storm's proximity to the Andhra Pradesh coast has brought the landfall forecast into focus. The IMD expects Murasu to continue moving northwestwards before crossing the coast as a severe cyclonic storm. Its projected landfall zone is between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole, with the crossing likely to begin around 11:30 pm on November 2 and continue into the early hours of November 3. The forecast wind speed is 100–110 kmph, with gusts reaching 120 kmph.Cyclone Murasu tracker: Landfall forecast and expected wind speedThe IMD has forecast that Murasu will maintain its northwestward movement towards the southern Andhra Pradesh coastline. The system is expected to cross the coast as a severe cyclonic storm, bringing strong winds to the landfall region.The projected wind speed of 100–110 kmph, with gusts of up to 120 kmph, could affect areas along the coast during the passage of the storm. The landfall window extends from late Monday night, November 2, to early Tuesday morning, November 3.Cyclone Murasu tracker: Heavy rainfall forecast in Odisha, NDRF and ODRAF on standbyThe IMD has forecast rainfall of 7–20 cm in southern Odisha districts on November 2 and 3 under the influence of the cyclone. Wind speeds in the state are also expected to reach 50–60 kmph, with gusts of up to 70 kmph on November 3.The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) personnel have been kept ready in vulnerable locations to respond to emergencies. items.title: Gross GST collections rise 23% to ₹2.31 trillion in October on strong sales
items.summary:
Gross GST collections increased 23 per cent to over Rs 2.31 lakh crore in October, driven by strong mop-up from domestic activities and imports, according to government data released on Sunday.
Gross GST collections from domestic sales rose 16 per cent to over Rs 1.59 lakh crore, and revenues from imports climbed 42 per cent to Rs 72,246 crore.
The Rs 2.31 lakh crore collection includes Central GST mop-up of 42,935 crore, State GST of Rs 51,340 crore and Integrated GST of over Rs 1.37 lakh crore, data showed.
Goods and Services Tax (GST) refunds increased 6.5 per cent year-on-year to Rs 27,934 crore in October.
After adjusting for refunds, net GST collections rose 26 per cent to over Rs 2.03 lakh crore in October.
During April-October, gross GST collection grew 13.2 per cent to over Rs 14.77 lakh crore. Net collections rose 13 per cent to over Rs 12.69 lakh crore.

items.title: AI bargains with AI: The next great bazaar
items.summary: In the market, humans meet humans to buy, sell and make deals. The next great bazaar may be where our Al agents haggle for milliseconds Walk through any Indian bazaar and bargaining is de rigueur. The shopkeeper names a price with wounded dignity, the buyer laughs derisively, threatens to walk away, comes back, talks about another shop and, eventually, both parties settle somewhere between offence and satisfaction. The transaction seems purely economic, but it is also social, rich in stories and psychological and emotional, and very human.Now imagine if neither of them is human.Also read: E-commerce firms turn to AI to solve for Bharat during festive salesYour AI agent has already discovered the product, compared alternatives, checked reviews and decided what you are willing to pay. The seller's AI knows inventory, margins, demand and how badly it needs the sale. The two agents bargain for milliseconds, settle on a price and complete the transaction. You receive a message: "Bought it. Saved you 12%."This is no longer science fiction. Personal agents such as Instinct, Meta's Muse and Open AI's Dots are moving AI from answering questions to doing things on our behalf, as you move from asking the AI to tasking the AI.Muse can browse, book and buy with permission. Instinct, which lives inside your WhatsApp, can arrange travel, buy groceries and manage subscriptions.Open AI's Dots are designed as always-on agents with their own cloud computers and access to connected applications. These are early steps towards what an agent really means: software to which we give agency.Also read: AI-aided gifting, self-love light up Zoomer DiwaliEra of negotiationThe next step is obvious. Why merely search and buy when the agent can negotiate? That possibility has moved from speculation to serious research. The Financial Times recently reported that Anthropic is consulting lawyers on how AI agents should negotiate for users, including prices, contracts and disputes.Experiments found that more aggressive agents sometimes got better outcomes, while cooperative ones occasionally gave up individual advantage to reach an agreement. Visa is already talking about "business-to-AI" commerce; more than half the business leaders it surveyed said they were ready for AI-to-AI negotiation.This could change commerce more profoundly than another shopping chatbot.First, the internet itself will have to change. Amazon, Flipkart, or a B2B procurement platform, is designed today to persuade humans. There are glossy pictures, seductive descriptions, stories, influencer videos, recommendations and carefully designed buttons. Machines care much less about romance. An agent wants structured facts: price, dimensions, warranty, delivery time, return policy, reliability, compatibility and perhaps the seller's willingness to negotiate.Two facesWebsites may therefore acquire two faces: one for humans, rich in stories and emotion, and another for machines, factual, structured and instantly comparable. Search engine optimisation gave us SEO. Agentic commerce may give us something like AEO: agent-engine optimisation. The next customer arriving at your website may never see the website.Bargaining itself becomes democratised. There are people who hate negotiating. A skilled agent could give an ordinary consumer some of the power previously available mainly to corporations and wealthy people - a tireless professional negotiator that knows when to push, when to walk away and what alternatives exist.But that creates a new inequality. What happens when my agent is smarter than yours? The wealthy have always hired better lawyers, brokers and advisers. If the richest people also subscribe to the most capable negotiating models, AI might not remove bargaining inequality but actually industrialise it.This is where John Nash and his famous work on game theory enter the bazaar. Game theory studies how rational actors behave when each person's outcome depends partly on what others do. A Nash equilibrium occurs when neither side gains by changing strategy alone.Human negotiators reach such equilibrium imperfectly, clouded by emotion, incomplete information and ego. AI agents could run thousands of strategies almost instantly.Collusion ConundrumBut there is a darker version. What if the buyer's agent and seller's agent learn that subtle cooperation is more profitable for both agents? Perhaps that is the choice ahead. Agents will increasingly represent us because, for many transactions, they will simply be better at it. They will know our budgets, preferences and histories, and eventually negotiate with other agents that know equally much about the other side.Algorithmic pricing has already raised concerns about tacit collusion. A world of autonomous negotiators makes the question sharper: whose interests are they really optimising?And then there is something less economic but perhaps equally important. Humans like shopping. We wander through bazaars, browse bookstores, discover things we did not know we wanted, argue over carpets and feel triumphant when a shopkeeper finally gives us "the special price only for you". Shopping is not merely procurement. It is entertainment, discovery, status, ritual and human contact.If my agent buys my airline ticket, insurance policy and printer cartridge, I will probably be delighted. If it chooses every restaurant, negotiates every holiday and buys every gift, I may have outsourced not just inconvenience but part of life itself.Perhaps that is the choice ahead. Agents will increasingly repre-sent us because, for many transactions, they will simply be better at it. They will know our budgets, preferences and histories, and eventually negotiate with other agents that know equally much about the other side.The bazaar will not disappear. It may split in two. In one, humans will still wander, haggle, flirt with choices and occasionally overpay for the pleasure of the experience. In the other, invisible agents will negotiate billions of transactions at machine speed.For thousands of years, the market was where humans met humans to bargain. The next great bazaar may be where our machines meet instead.
